title: Debate: agreeing, conceding and disagreeing politely
intro: Iranians love a good argument – and they wrap it in courtesy. In this lesson you learn to give your opinion strongly or softly, to agree, to concede a point (قبول دارم، ولی…), to disagree without giving offence, to interrupt politely (ببخشید که وسط حرفتان می‌پرم), to ask what someone means and to sum up. You follow a team meeting about working from home, read a newspaper column on city and village, and collect thirty debate phrases with their register.
goals: give an opinion strongly or softly, with the right verb form after each phrase
agree, concede and disagree politely: حق با شماست، قبول دارم ولی…، از یک طرف… از طرف دیگر
interrupt, ask for clarification and sum up a discussion
choose formal, neutral or informal phrases to suit the situation

sections.title: Should we work from home?
sections.context: Dariush leads a team meeting at a software company in Tehran. The company wants to decide about remote work (دورکاری), and he asks Reza and Sara for their views. Colleagues use شما with each other at work; listen for how they agree, concede, interrupt and sum up.

lines.fa: خب، دوستان، شرکت می‌خواهد درباره‌ی دورکاری تصمیم بگیرد. نظر شما چیست؟ دو روز در هفته از خانه کار کنیم یا نه؟
lines.r: khob, dustān, sherkat mi-khāhad darbāre-ye dur-kāri tasmim begirad. nazar-e shomā chist? do ruz dar hafte az khāne kār konim yā na?
lines.en: Right, everyone, the company wants to decide about remote work. What do you think? Should we work from home two days a week or not?
lines.col: خب، دوستان، شرکت می‌خواد درباره‌ی دورکاری تصمیم بگیره. نظرتون چیه؟ هفته‌ای دو روز از خونه کار کنیم یا نه؟
lines.colR: khob, dustān, sherkat mi-khād darbāre-ye dur-kāri tasmim begire. nazar-etun chiye? hafte-i do ruz az khune kār konim yā na?

lines.fa: من کاملاً موافقم! به نظر من دورکاری بدون شک بهتر است. هر روز دو ساعت در ترافیک تهران وقتم هدر می‌رود.
lines.r: man kāmelan movāfegh-am! be nazar-e man dur-kāri bedun-e shak behtar ast. har ruz do sā'at dar terāfik-e Tehrān vaght-am hadar mi-ravad.
lines.en: I completely agree! In my opinion remote work is without doubt better. Every day I waste two hours in Tehran traffic.
lines.col: من کاملاً موافقم! به نظرم دورکاری بی‌شک بهتره. هر روز دو ساعت تو ترافیک تهرون وقتم هدر می‌ره.
lines.colR: man kāmelan movāfegh-am! be nazar-am dur-kāri bi-shak behtar-e. har ruz do sā'at tu terāfik-e Tehrun vaght-am hadar mi-re.

lines.fa: ببخشید، ولی من این‌طور فکر نمی‌کنم. کار تیمی فقط با ایمیل و پیام پیش نمی‌رود.
lines.r: bebakhshid, vali man in-towr fekr nemi-konam. kār-e timi faghat bā imeyl va payām pish nemi-ravad.
lines.en: Sorry, but I don't see it that way. Teamwork doesn't get done with just emails and messages.
lines.col: ببخشید، ولی من این‌طوری فکر نمی‌کنم. کار تیمی فقط با ایمیل و پیام پیش نمی‌ره.

lines.en: I accept that face-to-face meetings matter, but…

lines.colR: ghabul dāram ke jalase-ye hozuri mohem-e, vali…

lines.fa: ببخشید که وسط حرفتان می‌پرم، ولی فقط جلسه نیست. وقتی همه در دفتر هستیم، مشکل‌ها را در پنج دقیقه حل می‌کنیم.

lines.en: Sorry to cut in, but it isn't just meetings. When we're all in the office, we solve problems in five minutes.

lines.r: yek lahze, Sārā jān. manzur-etān in ast ke dar khāne kam-tar kār mi-konim?
lines.en: Just a moment, Sara. Do you mean that we work less at home?

lines.en: No, that's not what I mean. I mean that communication gets weaker and you feel lonely.

lines.colR: na, manzur-am in nist. manzur-am in-e ke ertebāt za'if-tar mi-she o ādam ehsās-e tanhāyi mi-kone.

lines.fa: حق با شماست، تنهایی واقعاً مشکل است. ولی به نظرم کسی که دو ساعت در ترافیک نمانده، با انرژی بیشتری کار می‌کند.

lines.en: You're right, loneliness really is a problem. But I think someone who hasn't sat in traffic for two hours works with more energy.
lines.col: حق با شماست، تنهایی واقعاً مشکله. ولی به نظرم کسی که دو ساعت تو ترافیک نمونده، با انرژی بیشتری کار می‌کنه.

lines.r: āghā Rezā, mi-shavad yek mesāl bezanid?
lines.en: Reza, could you give us an example?
lines.col: آقا رضا، می‌شه یه مثال بزنین؟
lines.colR: āghā Rezā, mi-she ye mesāl bezanin?

lines.fa: بله. پارسال سه ماه از خانه کار کردم و بیشتر از همیشه کار انجام دادم. البته قبول دارم که گاهی دلم برای همکارها تنگ می‌شد.
lines.r: bale. pārsāl se māh az khāne kār kardam va bishtar az hamishe kār anjām dādam. albatte ghabul dāram ke gāhi del-am barā-ye hamkār-hā tang mi-shod.
lines.en: Yes. Last year I worked from home for three months and got more done than ever. Though I admit I sometimes missed my colleagues.
lines.col: آره. پارسال سه ماه از خونه کار کردم، از همیشه بیشتر کار انجام دادم. البته قبول دارم که گاهی دلم واسه همکارا تنگ می‌شد.

lines.fa: دقیقاً! خودتان هم گفتید: دلتان تنگ می‌شد. یعنی دورکاری برای همه مناسب نیست.
lines.r: daghighan! khod-etān ham goftid: del-etān tang mi-shod. ya'ni dur-kāri barā-ye hame monāseb nist.
lines.en: Exactly! You said it yourself: you missed them. That means remote work isn't right for everyone.

lines.fa: خب، بیایید جمع‌بندی کنیم: از یک طرف، دورکاری در وقت و انرژی ما صرفه‌جویی می‌کند؛ از طرف دیگر، ارتباط تیم را ضعیف می‌کند.

lines.en: Right, let's sum up: on the one hand, remote work saves our time and energy; on the other hand, it weakens communication in the team.

sections.title: The moves of a debate
sections.md:
Listen to the meeting again and you will hear the moves that every debate is made of:

1. **Giving an opinion** – strongly ([[کاملاً موافقم|kāmelan movāfegh-am]], [[بدون شک|bedun-e shak]]) or softly ([[به نظرم|be nazar-am]], [[شاید|shāyad]]).
2. **Disagreeing politely** – with an apology first: [[ببخشید، ولی من این‌طور فکر نمی‌کنم|bebakhshid, vali man in-towr fekr nemi-konam]].
3. **Conceding** – giving the other side a point before making your own: [[قبول دارم که…، ولی…|ghabul dāram ke…, vali…]], [[حق با شماست، ولی…|hagh bā shomā-st, vali…]].
4. **Interrupting** – [[ببخشید که وسط حرفتان می‌پرم|bebakhshid ke vasat-e harf-etān mi-param|sorry to jump into the middle of your words]].
5. **Asking for clarification** – [[منظورتان این است که…؟|manzur-etān in ast ke…?|do you mean that…?]], [[می‌شود یک مثال بزنید؟|mi-shavad yek mesāl bezanid?|could you give an example?]]
6. **Summing up** – [[بیایید جمع‌بندی کنیم|biyāyid jam'-bandi konim|let's sum up]], [[از یک طرف…، از طرف دیگر…|az yek taraf…, az taraf-e digar…|on the one hand…, on the other…]].

Notice that the colleagues use [[شما|shomā]] and the polite endings with each other although they are friends – normal at work in Iran. With close friends the same phrases go into the [[تو|to]] form: [[حق با توست|hagh bā to-st]], [[منظورت چیست؟|manzur-at chist?]]

Three words to keep apart: a [[بحث|bahs]] is any discussion or argument; a [[مناظره|monāzere]] is a formal debate, on a stage or on television; a [[دعوا|da'vā]] is a quarrel – the thing a good debate avoids.

ex.fa: قبول دارم که حق با شماست.
ex.r: ghabul dāram ke hagh bā shomā-st.

sections.title: Strong and soft: how sure are you?
sections.md:
How sure you are shows not only in the words but in the **verb after که**. When you are sure, it is the ordinary (indicative) verb; as soon as you express doubt, possibility or hope, it switches to the **subjunctive**:

- [[مطمئنم که می‌آید|motma'en-am ke mi-āyad|I'm sure he's coming]] – but [[فکر نمی‌کنم که بیاید|fekr nemi-konam ke biyāyad|I don't think he'll come]].
- [[شاید|shāyad|perhaps]], [[ممکن است|momken ast|it may be]], [[بعید است|ba'id ast|it's unlikely]] and [[امیدوارم|omidvār-am|I hope]] are always followed by the subjunctive.

To make an opinion **stronger**, add [[واقعاً|vāghe'an|really]], [[حتماً|hatman|definitely]] or [[بدون شک|bedun-e shak|without doubt]], or put [[اصلاً|aslan]] / [[به هیچ وجه|be hich vajh]] before a negative verb: *not at all*. To make it **softer**, put a cushion in front: [[به نظرم|be nazar-am|I think]], [[تا حدی|tā hadd-i|up to a point]], [[یک کم|yek kam|a bit]], [[احتمالاً|ehtemālan|probably]] – or turn it into a question: [[فکر نمی‌کنید که…؟|fekr nemi-konid ke…?|don't you think that…?]]

Iranians soften a lot. A flat [[اشتباه می‌کنید|eshtebāh mi-konid|you're wrong]] sounds rude in most settings; [[فکر می‌کنم یک کم اغراق می‌کنید|fekr mi-konam yek kam eghrāgh mi-konid|I think you're exaggerating a bit]] says the same and keeps the friendship.

sections.title: Conceding: قبول دارم، ولی… and از یک طرف… از طرف دیگر
sections.md:
In a good argument you rarely just agree or disagree – you **concede** a point and then add your own. Persian has a whole toolkit for this:

- **Yes, but:** [[قبول دارم که…، ولی…|ghabul dāram ke…, vali…|I accept that…, but…]], [[درست است که…، اما…|dorost ast ke…, ammā…|it's true that…, but…]], [[حق با شماست، ولی…|hagh bā shomā-st, vali…|you're right, but…]].
- **Although:** [[با این‌که|bā in-ke]], [[اگرچه|agar-che]] and the more literary [[هر چند|har chand]] all mean *although*. The main clause often adds [[باز هم|bāz ham|still]] or even [[ولی|vali]] – Persian is happy to say *although…, but…*: [[با این‌که خسته بود، باز هم کار کرد|bā in-ke khaste bud, bāz ham kār kard|although he was tired, he still worked]].
- **Both sides:** [[از یک طرف…، از طرف دیگر…|az yek taraf…, az taraf-e digar…|on the one hand…, on the other hand…]]; in writing [[از یک سو…، از سوی دیگر…|az yek su…, az su-ye digar…]].
- **Even so:** [[با این حال|bā in hāl|even so, nevertheless]] and, more formally, [[با وجود این|bā vojud-e in|in spite of this]].

After all of these the verb stays in the ordinary indicative: you are admitting a fact, not doubting it.

sections.title: Thirty phrases for a debate
sections.md:
Here are thirty phrases that carry a debate from the first opinion to the final summary. The last column says where each one belongs: **formal** – meetings, interviews, television, or speaking to someone much older or more senior; **neutral** – safe almost everywhere; **informal** – friends and family only.

The phrases are written in the standard form; in speech they are pronounced the spoken way ([[می‌شود|mi-shavad]] → *mi-she*, [[بدهید|bedahid]] → *bedin*, [[حرفتان|harf-etān]] → *harf-etun*). The polite plural is used throughout; with a friend, switch to the [[تو|to]] forms: [[منظورت چیست؟|manzur-at chist?]]

sections.intro: A short opinion column in formal written Persian. It presents both sides – از یک سو… از سوی دیگر – concedes a point, and sums up. Compare its phrases with the spoken ones in the meeting.

sections.title: Arguing the Iranian way
sections.md:
**Sorry before you disagree.** Iranians rarely contradict someone head-on, least of all someone older or more senior. A disagreement usually arrives wrapped in an apology: [[ببخشید، ولی…|bebakhshid, vali…]], [[با عرض معذرت…|bā 'arz-e ma'zerat…|with apologies…]], or the wonderful [[جسارتاً|jesāratan]] – literally *with boldness*, that is, *if I may be so bold*. A younger colleague may even begin [[شما بزرگ‌تر هستید، ولی…|shomā bozorg-tar hastid, vali…|you are older than me, but…]].

**Your words, kindly spoken.** In a formal discussion people report the other side's words with the polite verb [[فرمودن|farmudan]] instead of [[گفتن|goftan]]: [[همان‌طور که فرمودید…|hamān-towr ke farmudid…|as you (so kindly) said…]]. It costs nothing, and it makes the *but* that follows much easier to accept.

**Arguing for fun.** Among friends the rules are reversed. Football (Esteghlal or Persepolis?), politics, prices and which city has the best kabab are national sports, argued loudly over tea – and nobody takes offence. Young people call a playful duel of words [[کل‌کل|kal-kal]]. When it has gone on long enough, someone ends it with [[بی‌خیال، چایی‌مون سرد شد!|bi-khiyāl, chāyi-mun sard shod!|forget it – our tea's gone cold!]]

**On television.** At election time, live debates between candidates – [[مناظره‌ی تلویزیونی|monāzere-ye televizyoni]] – are watched by millions, and their sharpest lines are quoted for weeks.

sections.title: Tips
items: Start soft, finish firm. به نظرم… is never wrong; save مطمئنم and بدون شک for things you can prove.
After شاید، ممکن است، بعید است and فکر نمی‌کنم که use the subjunctive: فکر نمی‌کنم بیاید. After مطمئنم که and می‌دانم که use the ordinary present: مطمئنم که می‌آید.
ولی and اما both mean 'but'; اما is a little more formal, ولی is what people say. For 'not X but Y' use بلکه: مسئله شهر نیست، بلکه زندگی است.
To interrupt, apologise first, and use the polite plural even with colleagues your own age: ببخشید که وسط حرفتان می‌پرم – in speech …وسط حرفتون می‌پرم.
Check that you have understood before you attack: یعنی می‌گویید که…؟ ('so you're saying…?') wins you time and respect.
Be careful with نه بابا! Among friends it is playful ('come off it!'), but to a boss or an older person it sounds dismissive.
